analysis.one_liner: Cuts the corporate tax rate and the tax rate on capital gains and dividends to 10%.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the federal corporate income tax rate from a top rate of 35% to a flat 10%, and cut the tax rate on capital gains and dividends for both individuals and corporations from 15% to 10%. It would also have made permanent the lower capital gains rates first enacted in 2003, which were otherwise scheduled to expire. The bill received no action beyond its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and investors who earn income from capital gains and dividends. Because capital gains and dividends are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households, the tax cut flows overwhelmingly to high earners and profitable companies.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the corporate tax with a flat 10% tax on corporate taxable income, down from a top rate of 35%, including for personal service corporations.
Lowers the individual capital gains rate from 15% to 10% and cuts the tax rate on corporate capital gains from 35% to 10%.
Removes the scheduled expiration of the 2003 capital gains rate cuts, making the reduced rates permanent.
Reduces withholding requirements on foreign persons selling U.S. investments to the new 10% rate.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, whose revenue would fall sharply from both rate cuts, leaving some combination of larger deficits, higher taxes elsewhere, or reduced government services for everyone else.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 10% and the capital gains rate from 15% to 10% would sharply reduce federal revenue, and the bill text contains no spending cuts or tax increases to replace the lost money.

The benefits are concentrated: corporate income and capital gains flow mainly to profitable companies and high-income households, so the tax relief would go disproportionately to the top of the income distribution rather than to wage earners.
The bill would also lower the rate inside the alternative minimum tax to match, locking the lower rates in even for taxpayers otherwise subject to that parallel tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are real but narrow: lower tax bills for corporations and for households earning capital gains and dividends. The costs are broad: a large drop in federal revenue with no offset, which would have to be made up through borrowing, other taxes, or spending cuts. The design concentrates the gains at the top while spreading the cost across everyone who relies on or eventually pays for the federal budget.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Tipton introduced the bill on March 14, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Twelve House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The Ways and Means Committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill; it received no further action for the rest of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill never advanced, so the 10% rates never took effect and the concentrated tax savings never materialized; the Treasury kept the revenue it would have lost.

for.name: Rep. Scott Tipton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut corporate and capital gains rates to 10% and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup, a hearing, or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so opposition was never recorded; all recorded support came from Republicans, with 12 House Republicans cosponsoring and no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill replaces the corporate income tax with a flat 10% on corporate profits, down from a top 35% rate. That revenue funds public services, so the corporate gain is a direct cost to the general budget. Had it passed, the general public would have had to make up the difference.

industries.industry: Shareholders earning capital gains and dividends
industries.note: The bill cuts the tax rate on capital gains and dividends from 15% to 10% and makes the reduced rates permanent. Investment income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, so the gain flows mainly to them while the lost revenue must be covered by everyone.

industries.industry: Professional service firms organized as corporations
industries.note: The bill explicitly cuts the personal service corporation rate from 35% to 10%, a targeted benefit for law, consulting, and similar firms that incorporate.
